# Why Meiosis Requires Two Divisions

Meiosis must divide twice to achieve its essential purpose: **reducing the chromosome number by half** so that gametes (sex cells) can combine during fertilization without doubling chromosomes each generation.

## The Two Divisions Explained

### **Meiosis I: Separation of Homologous Pairs**
- Homologous chromosomes (one from each parent) separate
- **Reduces chromosome number from diploid (2n) to haploid (n)**
- Results in two cells, each with half the chromosomes

### **Meiosis II: Separation of Sister Chromatids**
- Sister chromatids separate (like mitosis)
- **Produces 4 haploid cells total**
- Each gamete has single copies of each chromosome

## Why Two Are Necessary

| Goal | Single Division? | Two Divisions? |
|------|---|---|
| Reduce chromosome number | ❌ Would stay the same | ✓ Cuts it in half |
| Separate homologous pairs | ❌ Incomplete | ✓ Complete |
| Separate chromatids | ❌ Incomplete | ✓ Complete |
| Produce gametes | ❌ Diploid (wrong!) | ✓ Haploid (correct) |

## The Bottom Line

Without both divisions, gametes would have the full diploid number of chromosomes. When two gametes fused during fertilization, the offspring would have **double the chromosome number**, and this would continue doubling each generation—which is unsustainable.
